children: China's consumer and factory-gate prices edged higher in August, fueled by energy-market jitters tied to renewed tensions in the Middle East.

The producer-price index climbed 3.8% in August from a year earlier, accelerating from July's 3.5% increase, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed Wednesday. The figure topped the median 3.7% increase projected by economists in a Wall Street Journal poll.

Factory-gate prices have risen for the sixth month in a row, driven by soaring oil costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. The trend marks a stark reversal from an extended, three-plus-year slump that began in late 2022.
On a monthly basis, producer prices rose 0.4% in August, improving from July's 0.7% decline, shrugging off the impact from adverse weather conditions that disrupted factory activities nationwide.
Meanwhile, China's consumer price rose 0.8% from a year earlier, faster than July's 0.5% growth and in line with the 0.8% increase expected by economists surveyed in the WSJ poll.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 1.0% in August from a year earlier, inching up from a 0.9% gain in the previous month.

Despite the recent uptick in inflation, questions persist about whether China's current reflationary trajectory can be sustained once the boost from surging energy prices abates, particularly as the years-long property slump shows few signs of bottoming out.
The real-estate downturn, which began in 2021, has hammered a primary revenue source for local governments and dented private confidence, creating a drag on domestic demand.

Economists at Goldman Sachs note that stressed local government finances have generated multiple headwinds, including diminished fiscal support for growth, rising corporate arrears, delayed civil-servant salaries, stricter tax and fee collection, and elevated local credit risks.
"These pressures have weighed on local investment and consumption and reinforced a negative feedback loop." the economists said in a report Monday.

The Chinese government's recent decision to pivot from the country's traditional property pre-sales system could further strain the property sector. Under the traditional pre-sales system, developers sold residences before completion. This contributed to mounting developer debt and stalled construction on these unfinished homes sparked widespread dissent and mortgage boycotts.

Under a new model unveiled by Beijing late last month, developers will collect only a small initial deposit, granting buyers the right to walk away from a purchase if their homes are not delivered on time.

According to Moody's Ratings, while such reforms will help institutionalize a less leveraged, more delivery-focused property model, the changes represent a structural reform rather than a cyclical stimulus, offering limited support to near-term property sales and economic growth.

In the short term, "the transition will impose costs and add funding pressure that will fall unevenly across sectors, with weaker developers and land-dependent local governments under the most pressure." the rating firm said last week.
